title: Limit Access to Resource Over Network
shortTitle: Limit Access to Resource Over Network
summary: Limiting access to resources over the network is an authorisation mitigation applied to file shares, remote administration services, databases and internal web applications, so that only accounts with a documented business need can reach them. The mechanism combines network reachability with identity: gateways and brokers terminate the connection, authenticate the user or device, check authorisation and then proxy the session, which keeps the service itself off the general network. Real environments implement it through jump hosts and remote desktop gateways, virtual private network concentrators with narrow tunnel policies, zero trust network access brokers, share permissions reviewed by a data owner, and hardened service configurations that remove anonymous or legacy access. Evidence appears in gateway authentication logs, share access auditing and denied connection attempts, which often reveal scanning from an already compromised host. The misunderstanding is that the tunnel is itself the control; granting access to a whole network recreates the flat network problem, so entitlements should be narrow and tied to a named resource.

beginner.definition: This means letting people reach only the network resources they need for their job. A file share, a database or a remote desktop session stays closed to everybody else. Access is granted to named accounts and checked again and again, not once for the whole network.
beginner.whyItMatters: If every account can reach every server, one stolen password opens the whole company. Restricting access means a compromised account can only touch a small area. It also removes old habits, such as open file shares that anyone can read. The result is less to protect, and fewer places for an attacker to hide.
howItWorks: List each network resource and note which teams truly need to use it.
Put a gateway in front of the resource, so users connect to the gateway first.
Check the user identity and permission each time before the session starts.
Remove anonymous access and old protocols that cannot support proper checks.
Log every connection, both the ones you allow and the ones you refuse.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital records office. You cannot walk straight to the shelves. You stop at a reception desk, show your badge, and explain which file you need. The clerk checks your name against a list and brings that one folder. Some staff may enter the back room, but only with a specific reason. Network resource access follows the same pattern: the gateway is the reception desk, and the list is your permission.
takeaways: A network tunnel should lead to a specific resource, not to the whole network.
Review share permissions with the data owner, because open shares grow quietly over time.
Denied connection logs show internal scanning before an attacker moves any further.

objectives: Explain the difference between network reachability and authorised access.
Describe how gateways and brokers mediate sessions to internal resources.
Identify legacy services and anonymous access that bypass permission checks.
Outline a permission review process owned by data owners.
Interpret denied access logs as an indicator of internal reconnaissance.
